column1: SECTION — HOTS OBSERVATION FRAMEWORK (16 Indicators | 1/2/3 Scale | Equal Weighting | Aligned with FICO)

column3: Discussions are teacher-dominated with minimal student input. Students respond only when directly called upon.
column4: Some encouragement for discussions, but student participation is limited and inconsistent.
column5: Open discussions are encouraged, with students freely sharing and debating ideas. Critical thinking is embedded in interactions.

column3: Resources and space are disorganised, limiting collaborative learning.
column4: Some organisation, but space/resources do not fully support collaborative tasks.
column5: Resources and space are well-organised for collaborative tasks. Tables arranged for group work.

column3: Students are given basic tasks without clear expectations. Instructions unclear.
column4: Some students engage in complex tasks, but expectations are not consistently communicated.
column5: Students actively participate in complex, clearly defined tasks. Success criteria stated upfront.

column3: Objectives are vague or focused on rote learning. Example: "Understand the topic."
column4: Objectives mention higher-order skills but lack detailed alignment with HOTS verbs.
column5: Objectives are explicit and linked to HOTS. Example: "Evaluate the author's argument using textual evidence."

column3: Strategies focus on recall and comprehension. Activities ask for definitions or facts only.
column4: Some activities promote analysis or synthesis but lack variety or depth.
column5: Strategies explicitly foster HOTS including evaluation and synthesis. Multiple Bloom's levels in one lesson.

column3: Lessons are taught in isolation without real-world relevance.
column4: Some connections to real-world themes, but not fully embedded in activities.
column5: Lessons integrate real-world applications and interdisciplinary links. Students apply learning to their context.

column3: Questions are mostly close-ended, requiring one-word answers. Example: "What is the capital?"
column4: Some open-ended questions are asked, but they lack depth. Example: "Why is the earth round?"
column5: Open-ended, thought-provoking questions dominate. Example: "How would the story change if the character made a different choice?"

column3: Students passively receive information. Teacher explains everything without student input.
column4: Some analysis and critique are encouraged, but not consistent across the lesson.
column5: Students actively analyse, interpret, and critique content. Students challenge ideas with evidence.

column3: Simple tasks demonstrated without explanation of the problem-solving process.
column4: Problem-solving is modelled, but the teacher does not explain strategies or invite students to try.
column5: Problem-solving and creativity are modelled with clear strategies. Students are invited to attempt their own approaches.

column3: Minimal or no scaffolding. Students asked to solve problems without support.
column4: Some scaffolding provided, but inconsistent. Support does not adjust to student needs.
column5: Effective scaffolding supports student exploration. Multiple tools: sentence frames, graphic organisers, think-alouds.

column3: Collaboration is minimal or absent. Students work individually throughout.
column4: Some collaboration occurs, but tasks lack depth. Students share ideas but don't synthesise.
column5: Collaboration is structured and focused on synthesis and problem-solving. Groups produce joint outputs.

column3: Content is presented from a single perspective. No alternative viewpoints explored.
column4: Multiple perspectives are mentioned, but exploration is limited. Teacher-led only.
column5: Students actively explore and evaluate multiple perspectives. Novel solutions encouraged and celebrated.

column3: Discussions are teacher-led with limited student involvement.
column4: Some discussions occur, but only a few students participate actively.
column5: Discussions and debates actively involve all students. Students collaborate and build on each other's ideas.

column3: Assessment limited to teacher-led grading. Students receive a grade with no self-reflection.
column4: Some self- or peer-assessment occurs, but inconsistent. No structured criteria provided.
column5: Self- and peer-assessment are structured and purposeful. Students use rubrics to evaluate reasoning.

column3: Feedback is generic: "Good job" or "Try again" with no specifics.
column4: Feedback is specific but does not consistently guide improvement.
column5: Feedback is specific, actionable, and focused on improvement. Example: "Your argument would be stronger with evidence from paragraph 3."

column3: Assessment tasks focus on recall only. No higher-order thinking required.
column4: Some tasks involve analysis or evaluation but lack depth.
column5: Assessment tasks consistently require analysis, evaluation, or creation.

column3: Grade groups work in isolation. No cross-grade interaction or peer teaching.
column4: Some cross-grade moments but not structured. Older students occasionally help younger.
column5: Structured cross-grade HOTS activities. Older students teach younger. Peer learning is planned.

column1: Domain Score = Average of indicators. Overall = Average of domains. Normalize: ((score-1)/2) × 100. Equal weighting.

1/2/3 (Emerging/Developing/Proficient) maps cleanly to FICO's 1-4 scale: • HOTS 1 (Emerging) = FICO 1 (Not Observed / Emerging) • HOTS 2 (Developing) = FICO 2 (Developing) • HOTS 3 (Proficient) = FICO 3-4 (Proficient)
